newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Great Eagle hotel deal positive--analysts.
newsitem.headline: Great Eagle hotel deal positive--analysts.

text.p: Great Eagle Holdings Ltd's purchase of a Melbourne hotel was a positive move and further bolstered buy recommendations on the company's stock, analysts said on Tuesday.
Great Eagle said on Monday it was in the process of acquiring a commercial complex in Melbourne, which included a 386-room hotel, two office blocks, and a shopping arcade.
Analysts said the purchase was expected to be completed in the coming three months.

Priced at A$119 million, or HK$1.88 million per room, Great Eagle management expects to see a yield of 7.5 percent in 1996, rising to 10 percent in 1997, said Raymond Ngai, senior investment analyst at UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd.
The high yield derives partly from the fact the hotel has a high occupancy rate of an average 82 percent per year, he said.
In May, Great Eagle bought the Langham Hilton in London for 100 million sterling. The five-star hotel has 380 rooms and operating income of 7.5 million pounds sterling in 1995.
The London and Melbourne acquisitions have been financed 70 percent by bank borrowings and 30 percent from internal company resources, analysts said.

"The company has used the same strategy in both cases. The hotels offer yields of around 10 percent while the funding cost is about 7.0 percent in both cases," said Adrian Ngan, director and property analyst at Peregrine Securities.
Great Eagle said in June it would continue to look for other hotel investments in Hong Kong, the United States and China. It has one China hotel project pending in Chengdu in Sechuan.
The company owns two hotels in Hong Kong, the five-star Hong Kong Renaissance Hotel and the four-star Eaton Hotel.

Construction is also underway on an urban redevelopment project in which the group has an undisclosed profit-sharing agreement with the Hong Kong government's Land Development Corporation (LDC). The partners have recently amended the plans of this project to include an 800-room hotel.
"The company needs to raise HK$2.0 billion to HK$3.0 billion to finance this project," said Ngai, adding that a spinoff of assets was the only way to raise such a large sum.

Great Eagle has previously said it wanted to spin off its investment property portfolio into a separate listing. But it was unlikely to sell these property assets at the current low level, analysts said.
The shares tumbled HK$0.35 to HK$27.85 on Tuesday, on top of a HK$0.70 drop on Monday, but analysts were not too concerned.
The share afterall broke above HK$25.00 in early November for the first time in three years and kept rising since then, though it remains well below its January 1994 peak of HK$40.25.
"The shares have risen with the general breakout of the property investment sector," said Peregrine's Ngan.
The higher the share climbs and the closer it comes to its NAV (net asset value) of HK$39.00, the more likely a spinoff of its investment properties becomes, he added.
Ngai calculates a NAV of HK$35.60 for the stock.

"Great Eagle is trading at a 20 percent discount to its NAV and I don't think management would like to sell them (its investment properties) so cheap," said UBS' Ngai. "With the spin-off of some assets still to come, the share should be considered a trading buy."
-- Kathleen Kearney (852) 2843 6933
